text: In their 1988 critique 'Connectionism and Cognitive Architecture,' Fodor and Pylyshyn argue that connectionist networks fail to explain the systematicity of thought -- the fact that anyone who can think 'John loves Mary' can think 'Mary loves John.' Their point is that connectionist networks:
choices: can never be trained to process any novel sentence at all
explain systematicity better than classical systems because they generalise from data
at best explain systematicity as an accidental by-product of training rather than as a structural guarantee of the architecture
presuppose an innate Mentalese and so beg the question against empiricism
explanation: Fodor and Pylyshyn concede a network might happen to handle 'Mary loves John' after training, but nothing in a distributed representation makes systematicity necessary -- it is not guaranteed by constituent structure as in a compositional classical system. Option 0 overstates the claim (networks can process novel inputs); option 1 inverts the argument; option 3 confuses this with the separate concept-nativism debate.
